memory_update.text: POWL should remain in the Layer 1B universe as a direct electrical-equipment chokepoint with disclosed data-center mega-order evidence; later layers must test repeatability, margin conversion, and customer concentration.

IESC is a plausible underfollowed execution-capacity candidate because data-center electrical contracting and integrated systems installation can become a bottleneck even when equipment is available; evidence is currently less granular than POWL.

LEU belongs in the nuclear-fuel-cycle shadow lane: direct exposure to data-center power is indirect, but HALEU/enrichment scarcity could matter if hyperscaler nuclear procurement and SMR projects advance.

Next search pass should look for smaller US-listed transformer, switchgear, substation, grid-testing, protection-relay, and EPC names below $10B market cap; the most direct public names found in this pass have already moved into large-cap territory or high-attention buckets.

POWL should remain a high-priority Layer 2 verification candidate for AI/data-center power infrastructure because it has direct backlog/order evidence tied to data-center electrical equipment, including a >$400 million order.

MYRG is a plausible underfollowed construction-capacity play on transmission, distribution, substations, and commercial data-center electrical work; next layer must separate AI/data-center demand from generic grid modernization.

ATKR belongs in the component/materials lane as a cable-management and conduit supplier, but the exposure is currently a hypothesis until data-center revenue contribution and margin durability are quantified.
ENS belongs in the backup-power/stored-energy lane; data-center product announcements are real, but materiality to revenue and competitive positioning need verification.

Later searches should add transformer manufacturers, turbine supply-chain names, substation components, grid-planning software, nuclear fuel/enrichment names, and local regulated utility assets, but this pass focused on scarce equipment, construction, cable-management, and backup-power suppliers.

POWL should remain a reference/purity check for AI data-center electrical equipment because company evidence shows direct data-center megaproject orders and backlog growth, but it may no longer be meaningfully underfollowed after the large order disclosure.

MYRG is a high-priority underfollowed contractor candidate for the grid/interconnection node; next layer should verify data-center and substation exposure inside C&I and transmission/distribution backlog.

PRIM is a plausible but lower-confidence second-order candidate: utility and power-delivery exposure fits the AI load-growth bottleneck, but direct data-center attribution and recent execution volatility require falsification work.

AZZ is a hidden-in-plain-sight infrastructure materials/services candidate; its galvanizing footprint may benefit from transmission, power and data-center construction, but AI-specific exposure is indirect and must be quantified.

For this node, the best underfollowed discovery path is not utilities themselves but switchgear, electrical construction, substations/transmission contractors, grid-hardening services, and boring materials/process bottlenecks such as galvanizing and power-infrastructure components.
Layer 2 should explicitly test whether backlog is tied to data-center load and interconnection work rather than generic construction, renewables, or cyclical industrial demand.

POWL has the clearest company-disclosed AI/data-center power evidence in this node via a >$400 million data-center electrical order and record backlog, but its market cap has expanded into large-cap territory and attention is rising.

IESC is a strong underfollowed electrical-infrastructure candidate: data-center demand is explicitly driving Communications and Infrastructure Solutions growth, but the company is now large-cap and needs customer/backlog mix verification.

MYRG maps to the transmission, distribution, substation, and electrical-construction layer of the AI power bottleneck; strongest next check is project geography/customer linkage to data-center load clusters.

ATKR is a lower-confidence second-order candidate in conduit/electrical infrastructure products; inclusion should depend on whether data-center demand is material enough to offset pricing, litigation, and non-AI cyclicality.

This pass did not expand nuclear fuel, turbine OEMs, utilities, IPPs, or transformer-only suppliers due to the four-candidate limit; future Layer 1B passes should separately map HALEU/enrichment, turbine backlogs, and transformer components.

node: Grid, power generation, transmission, and interconnection bottlenecks
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Layer 1B expands the directly exposed public-company universe for the AI/data-center power bottleneck. The strongest reference anchor is GE Vernova because gas-turbine slots, grid equipment, and electrification orders directly validate the node. The underfollowed lane should prioritize electrical equipment and project-execution chokepoints rather than only utilities or data-center REITs: Powell Industries for medium-voltage switchgear/e-houses and data-center electrical distribution, IES Holdings for electrical/data-center infrastructure execution capacity, and Centrus Energy as a nuclear-fuel-cycle bottleneck tied to advanced nuclear power availability. This is research mapping only, not a buy/sell recommendation. Layer 1B expands the universe around scarce grid/power equipment and construction capacity needed for AI/data-center load growth. The strongest underfollowed lane candidates are not hyperscalers or utilities, but medium-voltage switchgear makers, transmission/substation contractors, cable-management suppliers, and backup/stored-energy vendors. The current evidence points to transformers, switchgear, batteries, transmission construction, and interconnection-related equipment as physical bottlenecks; later layers should verify order durability, customer concentration, capacity expansion, margins, and whether AI/data-center demand is incremental versus replacing cyclical industrial demand.
